DocuSign Earnings Call Highlights AI-Led Growth Momentum
Tipranks - Tipranks - Wed Sep 16, 7:06PM CDT
Docusign ((DOCU)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.
DocuSign’s latest earnings call carried a distinctly upbeat tone, as management highlighted another quarter of solid growth and expanding profitability. Executives acknowledged minor pressures from cloud migration and foreign exchange, but these were framed as manageable trade‑offs against accelerating Intelligent Agreement Management adoption and strengthened customer metrics.
DocuSign reported Q2 revenue of $876 million, up 9% year-over-year, showcasing steady top-line momentum in a choppy software spending environment. The company delivered a robust 32% operating margin and nearly $300 million in free cash flow, enough to fund more than $300 million of share repurchases in the quarter.
Intelligent Agreement Management is swiftly becoming a core growth engine, accounting for 15.1% of total ARR in Q2 versus 12.6% in Q1. Management said IAM adoption slightly beat expectations, with strong traction across regions and segments, spanning both commercial users and larger enterprise customers.
Customers have now ingested more than 300 million documents into IAM’s Agreement Manager, highlighting rapid scale. DocuSign emphasized that IAM’s AI-native architecture runs workloads at much lower marginal cost than systems relying on external large language models, supporting this document surge while preserving high gross margins.
Expansion of AI and Agentic Capabilities
The company rolled out IAM AI Assistant and Agentic tools for contract analysis, redlining, workflow automation, and custom agents via Agent Studio. In testing, the AI assistant cut the time required to summarize, review, and finalize agreements such as NDAs by roughly half, underscoring tangible productivity gains for customers.
DocuSign expanded its ecosystem with a Slack app, plus integrations with Perplexity and several major AI platforms, including Gemini Enterprise for Legal. Management noted that cumulative active MCP accounts more than quadrupled during the quarter, and the DocuSign MCP server is expected to reach general availability late next year.
IAM Agreement Manager is now fully integrated into DocuSign CLM, allowing CLM customers to tap a single AI-driven repository for eSign and CLM data. This linkage connects CLM workflows with IAM’s AI-powered search, extraction, MCP connectivity, and Agentic suite, and early customer feedback was described as highly encouraging.
AI-assisted Web Forms became generally available, letting users convert static legacy documents into interactive, shareable forms. By unlocking the data trapped in those documents, DocuSign aims to deepen engagement and open up new automation and analytics use cases across its installed base.
Customer Wins Across Industries and Functions
The company highlighted new IAM wins at names like Salesforce, Oppenheimer, SailPoint, Upstart, Optimizely, and HydroCorp, spanning sales, onboarding, and borrower workflows. HydroCorp’s implementation cut contract preparation time from 2–3 hours to about 20 minutes, illustrating the efficiency improvements DocuSign’s AI stack can deliver.
Dollar net retention from direct customers ticked up to 103% from 102%, with management pointing to a more balanced mix of retention and expansion. The improvement suggests existing customers are not only sticking with DocuSign but also broadening usage, an important signal for long-term recurring revenue health.
Total customer growth accelerated to nearly 10% year-over-year, pushing the base to more than 1.9 million accounts overall. Digital channels were a particular bright spot, and management noted that both envelopes sent and contract utilization increased year-over-year, pointing to deeper platform engagement.
Growth in Larger Customers and Deal Sizes
Customers spending over $300,000 in ACV rose 14% year-over-year to nearly 1,300, marking a second straight quarter of double-digit expansion. The quarter also featured DocuSign’s largest deal ever in the U.S. public sector and its biggest deal to date in Latin America, underscoring growing enterprise demand.
Non-GAAP operating income climbed 16% year-over-year to $277 million, reflecting continued operating leverage. Non-GAAP operating margin reached 31.6%, improving 180 basis points year-over-year and coming in 160 basis points above the company’s guidance midpoint.
Non-GAAP diluted EPS came in at $1.16, up 26% year-over-year, while GAAP diluted EPS rose 33% to $0.40. Management attributed the EPS gains to stronger operating performance, lower stock-based compensation, and a smaller share count after recent buybacks.
Free cash flow for Q2 was $296 million, up more than 35% year-over-year and representing a 34% margin. On a trailing 12-month basis, free cash flow reached $1.2 billion, almost triple full-year fiscal 2023 levels, driven by improving leverage and tighter working capital management.
Strong Balance Sheet and Shareholder Returns
DocuSign ended the quarter with just under $1 billion in cash, equivalents, and investments and no debt on the balance sheet. The company repurchased $307 million of stock in Q2, cutting diluted shares outstanding by 8% year-over-year, with $2.1 billion still available under its repurchase authorization.
Improved Stock-Based Compensation Efficiency
Stock-based compensation fell to 17% of revenue in Q2, improving 3 percentage points versus last year. This shift supports better alignment between employee incentives and shareholder returns while reducing a key source of EPS dilution.
Continued Targeted Investment With Cost Discipline
Management stressed that DocuSign is investing heavily in innovation and IAM while tightly controlling hiring and resources. The Docusign IAM platform unifies and automates every stage of the agreement lifecycle from intake and contract creation to identity verification, e-signature, and ongoing management of executed agreements. "Docusign's new platform evolution, framed as Intelligent Agreement Management, reflects how AI-powered contract management is reshaping enterprise workflows," said Andrew Gens, research analyst for AI software at IDC. "Agreements are the foundation of business, yet traditional processes leave valuable data locked inside static files. Our IAM platform empowers organizations to turn agreement friction into business results, delivering tangible ROI and efficiency across teams like legal, sales, procurement, and HR."
Among Docusign's key strengths, the IDC MarketScape cited breadth of the agreement lifecycle platform as well as its scale, contract AI, and ecosystem depth:
Scale and ecosystem depth: Docusign's broad installed base and library of over 1,000 prebuilt integrations affect enterprise procurement in practical terms. Internal stakeholders and counterparties are often already familiar with the platform, and integration into systems such as Salesforce, SAP, Microsoft, Google, and Coupa is well documented and broadly supported by systems integrator partners.
Breadth of the agreement life-cycle platform: Docusign has extended its platform to cover pre-execution and post-execution agreement management, AI-assisted contract analysis, and automated workflow orchestration. For organizations that want to consolidate agreement creation, signing, and life-cycle management under one vendor rather than assembling separate tools, this functional breadth can cover most of that scope directly.

Blake Jeffrey Grayson, Chief Financial Officer of DocuSign, Inc. (NASDAQ:DOCU), sold 45,000 shares of common stock between September 4, 2026 and September 8, 2026, according to a recent SEC Form 4 filing.

The shares were sold at a weighted average price of $68.52, while the stock was priced at $65.08 as of the September 8, 2026 market close, representing a one-year total return of -20% as of the transaction date.

DocuSign serves a broad customer base spanning mid-market and enterprise organizations across multiple verticals, with particular strength in financial services, legal, healthcare, and technology sectors seeking to streamline agreement processes.

CFO Blake Grayson's Sept. 4 sale of 30,000 DocuSign shares was a non-discretionary transaction executed as part of a pre-established Rule 10b5-1 plan. This indicates the move was part of a structured portfolio management strategy.

DocuSign Earnings Call Highlights AI-Led Growth Momentum
Tipranks - Tipranks - Wed Sep 16, 7:06PM CDT
Docusign ((DOCU)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.
DocuSign’s latest earnings call carried a distinctly upbeat tone, as management highlighted another quarter of solid growth and expanding profitability. Executives acknowledged minor pressures from cloud migration and foreign exchange, but these were framed as manageable trade‑offs against accelerating Intelligent Agreement Management adoption and strengthened customer metrics.
DocuSign reported Q2 revenue of $876 million, up 9% year-over-year, showcasing steady top-line momentum in a choppy software spending environment. The company delivered a robust 32% operating margin and nearly $300 million in free cash flow, enough to fund more than $300 million of share repurchases in the quarter.
Intelligent Agreement Management is swiftly becoming a core growth engine, accounting for 15.1% of total ARR in Q2 versus 12.6% in Q1. Management said IAM adoption slightly beat expectations, with strong traction across regions and segments, spanning both commercial users and larger enterprise customers.
Customers have now ingested more than 300 million documents into IAM’s Agreement Manager, highlighting rapid scale. DocuSign emphasized that IAM’s AI-native architecture runs workloads at much lower marginal cost than systems relying on external large language models, supporting this document surge while preserving high gross margins.
Expansion of AI and Agentic Capabilities
The company rolled out IAM AI Assistant and Agentic tools for contract analysis, redlining, workflow automation, and custom agents via Agent Studio. In testing, the AI assistant cut the time required to summarize, review, and finalize agreements such as NDAs by roughly half, underscoring tangible productivity gains for customers.
DocuSign expanded its ecosystem with a Slack app, plus integrations with Perplexity and several major AI platforms, including Gemini Enterprise for Legal. Management noted that cumulative active MCP accounts more than quadrupled during the quarter, and the DocuSign MCP server is expected to reach general availability late next year.
IAM Agreement Manager is now fully integrated into DocuSign CLM, allowing CLM customers to tap a single AI-driven repository for eSign and CLM data. This linkage connects CLM workflows with IAM’s AI-powered search, extraction, MCP connectivity, and Agentic suite, and early customer feedback was described as highly encouraging.
AI-assisted Web Forms became generally available, letting users convert static legacy documents into interactive, shareable forms. By unlocking the data trapped in those documents, DocuSign aims to deepen engagement and open up new automation and analytics use cases across its installed base.
Customer Wins Across Industries and Functions
The company highlighted new IAM wins at names like Salesforce, Oppenheimer, SailPoint, Upstart, Optimizely, and HydroCorp, spanning sales, onboarding, and borrower workflows. HydroCorp’s implementation cut contract preparation time from 2–3 hours to about 20 minutes, illustrating the efficiency improvements DocuSign’s AI stack can deliver.
Dollar net retention from direct customers ticked up to 103% from 102%, with management pointing to a more balanced mix of retention and expansion. The improvement suggests existing customers are not only sticking with DocuSign but also broadening usage, an important signal for long-term recurring revenue health.
Total customer growth accelerated to nearly 10% year-over-year, pushing the base to more than 1.9 million accounts overall. Digital channels were a particular bright spot, and management noted that both envelopes sent and contract utilization increased year-over-year, pointing to deeper platform engagement.
Growth in Larger Customers and Deal Sizes
Customers spending over $300,000 in ACV rose 14% year-over-year to nearly 1,300, marking a second straight quarter of double-digit expansion. The quarter also featured DocuSign’s largest deal ever in the U.S. public sector and its biggest deal to date in Latin America, underscoring growing enterprise demand.
Non-GAAP operating income climbed 16% year-over-year to $277 million, reflecting continued operating leverage. Non-GAAP operating margin reached 31.6%, improving 180 basis points year-over-year and coming in 160 basis points above the company’s guidance midpoint.
Non-GAAP diluted EPS came in at $1.16, up 26% year-over-year, while GAAP diluted EPS rose 33% to $0.40. Management attributed the EPS gains to stronger operating performance, lower stock-based compensation, and a smaller share count after recent buybacks.
Free cash flow for Q2 was $296 million, up more than 35% year-over-year and representing a 34% margin. On a trailing 12-month basis, free cash flow reached $1.2 billion, almost triple full-year fiscal 2023 levels, driven by improving leverage and tighter working capital management.
Strong Balance Sheet and Shareholder Returns
DocuSign ended the quarter with just under $1 billion in cash, equivalents, and investments and no debt on the balance sheet. The company repurchased $307 million of stock in Q2, cutting diluted shares outstanding by 8% year-over-year, with $2.1 billion still available under its repurchase authorization.
Improved Stock-Based Compensation Efficiency
Stock-based compensation fell to 17% of revenue in Q2, improving 3 percentage points versus last year. This shift supports better alignment between employee incentives and shareholder returns while reducing a key source of EPS dilution.
Continued Targeted Investment With Cost Discipline
Management stressed that DocuSign is investing heavily in innovation and IAM while tightly controlling hiring and resources. Headcount rose just 3% year-over-year to 7,137, all in lower-cost locations, even as operating margins climbed from the high teens four years ago to roughly 32% and revenue grew about 40%.
eSignature Market Position and Pricing Tests
Executives reiterated that eSignature remains the premium product in its category, with strong brand recognition, security, and regulatory acceptance worldwide. DocuSign is testing new pricing and packaging, including in Canada, where early results look promising though no broad price changes have yet been announced.
The digital team has been actively experimenting with conversion rates, customer quality, and pricing to refine its go-to-market. These efforts helped drive nearly 10% account growth in the quarter, reinforcing digital as a key acquisition and expansion channel.
Non-GAAP gross margin edged down to 81.7%, a modest year-over-year decline tied to ongoing cloud migration investments. Management said fiscal 2027 gross margins are also likely to dip slightly as the migration, which is still on track to finish largely by year-end, continues.
Q2 revenue growth benefited from a 1.3 percentage point tailwind from foreign exchange, but guidance reflects more mixed FX dynamics. For fiscal 2027, management expects roughly a 1 point FX benefit to growth, partially offset by about $4 million in incremental currency headwinds.
Digital Add-On Revenue Transition Creates Comparability Noise
DocuSign cautioned that revenue comparisons are somewhat noisy because of early renewals, digital add-ons, and services fees not captured in ARR. As the company transitions customers from usage-based digital add-ons to ratable subscription plans, reported revenue patterns may diverge temporarily from underlying ARR trends.
Some IAM Workflow Tools Require Longer Rollouts
Management noted that customers can deploy IAM’s intelligent repository quickly, but more complex workflow tools take longer to implement. Many enterprises need to rework internal processes before fully tapping IAM’s automation potential, extending rollout timetables for certain capabilities.
Connector Monetization and Discovery Are Still Early
DocuSign has launched connectors across platforms like Slack and OpenAI, yet these currently serve more as product extensions than revenue drivers. Executives said it remains early for connectors to function as fully developed buying or discovery channels, and incremental monetization is still limited.
While IAM is gaining traction, management emphasized that enterprise adoption is still in the early innings, with “green shoots” rather than broad-scale uptake. That leaves a sizeable runway ahead, but also means the revenue impact from large enterprises will build over time rather than immediately.
Full-Year Gross Margin Guidance Reduced Slightly Year-over-Year
For fiscal 2027, DocuSign now guides non-GAAP gross margin to 81.5%–82.0%, a slight decline versus the prior year. The company tied this modest compression squarely to the cloud migration, signaling that margin pressure is strategic and largely temporary.
For Q3, DocuSign expects revenue of $886–$890 million, about 9% growth at the midpoint, alongside gross margins near 81.5%–81.9% and operating margins above 31%. For fiscal 2027, revenue is guided to $3.499–$3.507 billion with ARR growth of 8.5%–9.0%, IAM rising to roughly 18%–19% of ARR, modest DNR improvement, and slightly lower gross margins as migration wraps.
DocuSign’s earnings call painted a picture of a company balancing innovation with disciplined execution, as AI-led products fuel growth on top of a durable eSignature franchise. For investors, the key takeaways were accelerating IAM adoption, expanding margins, strong cash generation, and cautiously optimistic guidance, offset only by manageable FX and migration-related margin noise.

Executives acknowledged minor pressures from cloud migration and foreign exchange, but these were framed as manageable trade‑offs against accelerating Intelligent Agreement Management adoption and strengthened customer metrics.
DocuSign reported Q2 revenue of $876 million, up 9% year-over-year, showcasing steady top-line momentum in a choppy software spending environment. The company delivered a robust 32% operating margin and nearly $300 million in free cash flow, enough to fund more than $300 million of share repurchases in the quarter.
Intelligent Agreement Management is swiftly becoming a core growth engine, accounting for 15.1% of total ARR in Q2 versus 12.6% in Q1. Management said IAM adoption slightly beat expectations, with strong traction across regions and segments, spanning both commercial users and larger enterprise customers.
Customers have now ingested more than 300 million documents into IAM’s Agreement Manager, highlighting rapid scale. DocuSign emphasized that IAM’s AI-native architecture runs workloads at much lower marginal cost than systems relying on external large language models, supporting this document surge while preserving high gross margins.
Expansion of AI and Agentic Capabilities
The company rolled out IAM AI Assistant and Agentic tools for contract analysis, redlining, workflow automation, and custom agents via Agent Studio. In testing, the AI assistant cut the time required to summarize, review, and finalize agreements such as NDAs by roughly half, underscoring tangible productivity gains for customers.
DocuSign expanded its ecosystem with a Slack app, plus integrations with Perplexity and several major AI platforms, including Gemini Enterprise for Legal. Management noted that cumulative active MCP accounts more than quadrupled during the quarter, and the DocuSign MCP server is expected to reach general availability late next year.
IAM Agreement Manager is now fully integrated into DocuSign CLM, allowing CLM customers to tap a single AI-driven repository for eSign and CLM data. This linkage connects CLM workflows with IAM’s AI-powered search, extraction, MCP connectivity, and Agentic suite, and early customer feedback was described as highly encouraging.
AI-assisted Web Forms became generally available, letting users convert static legacy documents into interactive, shareable forms. By unlocking the data trapped in those documents, DocuSign aims to deepen engagement and open up new automation and analytics use cases across its installed base.
Customer Wins Across Industries and Functions
The company highlighted new IAM wins at names like Salesforce, Oppenheimer, SailPoint, Upstart, Optimizely, and HydroCorp, spanning sales, onboarding, and borrower workflows. HydroCorp’s implementation cut contract preparation time from 2–3 hours to about 20 minutes, illustrating the efficiency improvements DocuSign’s AI stack can deliver.
Dollar net retention from direct customers ticked up to 103% from 102%, with management pointing to a more balanced mix of retention and expansion. The improvement suggests existing customers are not only sticking with DocuSign but also broadening usage, an important signal for long-term recurring revenue health.
Total customer growth accelerated to nearly 10% year-over-year, pushing the base to more than 1.9 million accounts overall. Digital channels were a particular bright spot, and management noted that both envelopes sent and contract utilization increased year-over-year, pointing to deeper platform engagement.
Growth in Larger Customers and Deal Sizes
Customers spending over $300,000 in ACV rose 14% year-over-year to nearly 1,300, marking a second straight quarter of double-digit expansion. The quarter also featured DocuSign’s largest deal ever in the U.S. public sector and its biggest deal to date in Latin America, underscoring growing enterprise demand.
Non-GAAP operating income climbed 16% year-over-year to $277 million, reflecting continued operating leverage. Non-GAAP operating margin reached 31.6%, improving 180 basis points year-over-year and coming in 160 basis points above the company’s guidance midpoint.
Non-GAAP diluted EPS came in at $1.16, up 26% year-over-year, while GAAP diluted EPS rose 33% to $0.40. Management attributed the EPS gains to stronger operating performance, lower stock-based compensation, and a smaller share count after recent buybacks.
Free cash flow for Q2 was $296 million, up more than 35% year-over-year and representing a 34% margin. On a trailing 12-month basis, free cash flow reached $1.2 billion, almost triple full-year fiscal 2023 levels, driven by improving leverage and tighter working capital management.
Strong Balance Sheet and Shareholder Returns
DocuSign ended the quarter with just under $1 billion in cash, equivalents, and investments and no debt on the balance sheet. The company repurchased $307 million of stock in Q2, cutting diluted shares outstanding by 8% year-over-year, with $2.1 billion still available under its repurchase authorization.
Improved Stock-Based Compensation Efficiency
Stock-based compensation fell to 17% of revenue in Q2, improving 3 percentage points versus last year. This shift supports better alignment between employee incentives and shareholder returns while reducing a key source of EPS dilution.
Continued Targeted Investment With Cost Discipline
Management stressed that DocuSign is investing heavily in innovation and IAM while tightly controlling hiring and resources. Headcount rose just 3% year-over-year to 7,137, all in lower-cost locations, even as operating margins climbed from the high teens four years ago to roughly 32% and revenue grew about 40%.
eSignature Market Position and Pricing Tests
Executives reiterated that eSignature remains the premium product in its category, with strong brand recognition, security, and regulatory acceptance worldwide. DocuSign is testing new pricing and packaging, including in Canada, where early results look promising though no broad price changes have yet been announced.
The digital team has been actively experimenting with conversion rates, customer quality, and pricing to refine its go-to-market. These efforts helped drive nearly 10% account growth in the quarter, reinforcing digital as a key acquisition and expansion channel.
Non-GAAP gross margin edged down to 81.7%, a modest year-over-year decline tied to ongoing cloud migration investments. Management said fiscal 2027 gross margins are also likely to dip slightly as the migration, which is still on track to finish largely by year-end, continues.
Q2 revenue growth benefited from a 1.3 percentage point tailwind from foreign exchange, but guidance reflects more mixed FX dynamics. For fiscal 2027, management expects roughly a 1 point FX benefit to growth, partially offset by about $4 million in incremental currency headwinds.
Digital Add-On Revenue Transition Creates Comparability Noise
DocuSign cautioned that revenue comparisons are somewhat noisy because of early renewals, digital add-ons, and services fees not captured in ARR. As the company transitions customers from usage-based digital add-ons to ratable subscription plans, reported revenue patterns may diverge temporarily from underlying ARR trends.
Some IAM Workflow Tools Require Longer Rollouts
Management noted that customers can deploy IAM’s intelligent repository quickly, but more complex workflow tools take longer to implement. Many enterprises need to rework internal processes before fully tapping IAM’s automation potential, extending rollout timetables for certain capabilities.
Connector Monetization and Discovery Are Still Early
DocuSign has launched connectors across platforms like Slack and OpenAI, yet these currently serve more as product extensions than revenue drivers. Executives said it remains early for connectors to function as fully developed buying or discovery channels, and incremental monetization is still limited.
While IAM is gaining traction, management emphasized that enterprise adoption is still in the early innings, with “green shoots” rather than broad-scale uptake. That leaves a sizeable runway ahead, but also means the revenue impact from large enterprises will build over time rather than immediately.
Full-Year Gross Margin Guidance Reduced Slightly Year-over-Year
For fiscal 2027, DocuSign now guides non-GAAP gross margin to 81.5%–82.0%, a slight decline versus the prior year. The company tied this modest compression squarely to the cloud migration, signaling that margin pressure is strategic and largely temporary.
For Q3, DocuSign expects revenue of $886–$890 million, about 9% growth at the midpoint, alongside gross margins near 81.5%–81.9% and operating margins above 31%. For fiscal 2027, revenue is guided to $3.499–$3.507 billion with ARR growth of 8.5%–9.0%, IAM rising to roughly 18%–19% of ARR, modest DNR improvement, and slightly lower gross margins as migration wraps.
DocuSign’s earnings call painted a picture of a company balancing innovation with disciplined execution, as AI-led products fuel growth on top of a durable eSignature franchise. For investors, the key takeaways were accelerating IAM adoption, expanding margins, strong cash generation, and cautiously optimistic guidance, offset only by manageable FX and migration-related margin noise.

San Francisco – September 3, 2026 – Docusign, Inc. (NASDAQ: DOCU) today announced results for its second fiscal quarter ended July 31, 2026. Prepared remarks and the news release with the financial results will be accessible on Docusign’s website at investor.docusign.com prior to its webcast.

Docusign Announces First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Financial Results
San Francisco – June 4, 2026 – Docusign, Inc. (NASDAQ: DOCU) today announced results for its fiscal quarter ended April 30, 2026. Prepared remarks and the news release with the financial results will be accessible on Docusign’s website at investor.docusign.com prior to its webcast.
"In Q1, we saw continued growing demand for Docusign’s AI-native IAM platform with 40,000 customers investing in our rapidly expanding roadmap,” said Allan Thygesen, CEO of Docusign. "We delivered significant innovation this quarter while driving strong financial results through durable revenue growth, substantial free cash flow, and record share buybacks.”
▪Revenue was $830.2 million, a 9% year-over-year increase including approximately 1.6% positive impact from foreign exchange rates.
▪Intelligent Agreement Management (“IAM”) represented 12.6% of our total Annual Recurring Revenue (“ARR”) as of April 30, 2026, compared to 10.8% of our total ARR as of January 31, 2026.
▪GAAP gross margin was 79.4% for both periods. Non-GAAP gross margin was 81.5% compared to 82.3% in the same period last year.
▪GAAP net income per basic share was $0.40 on 195 million shares outstanding compared to $0.35 on 203 million shares outstanding in the same period last year.
▪GAAP net income per diluted share was $0.40 on 196 million shares outstanding compared to $0.34 on 213 million shares outstanding in the same period last year.
▪Non-GAAP net income per diluted share was $1.09 on 196 million shares outstanding compared to $0.90 on 213 million shares outstanding in the same period last year.
▪Net cash provided by operating activities was $321.7 million compared to $251.4 million in the same period last year.
▪Free cash flow was $289.4 million compared to $227.8 million in the same period last year.
▪Cash, cash equivalents, and investments were $1.0 billion at the end of the quarter.
▪Repurchases of common stock were $317.5 million compared to $183.4 million in the same period last year.
A reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP financial measures has been provided in the tables included in this press release. An explanation of these measures is also included below under the heading “Non-GAAP Financial Measures and Other Key Metrics.”
AI-Powered Intelligent Agreement Management (“IAM”) announcements: In May at our annual Momentum conference, Docusign announced new IAM capabilities powered by Iris, our agreement AI engine:
Iris assistant and agents: Iris is Docusign’s AI engine for agreements, which helps teams work smarter, faster, and trigger actions using natural language. Customers can now:
•Move faster through reviews: Agents can check agreements against company standards, suggest edits, and automatically request the right approvals in minutes.
•Keep work moving automatically: Agents can monitor contracts in the background and flag risks, track obligations, and trigger next steps without manual follow-up.
•Build agents for specific workflows: With Docusign Agent Studio, teams can create and deploy custom agents tailored to how they manage deals, renewals, approvals, and more.
Docusign IAM platform ecosystem: Docusign connects agreement work across the systems and teams that run the business. Instead of contracts living in silos, Docusign brings them into the tools people already use:
•AI where teams work: Through our open platform and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, Docusign connects with leading frontier models like Anthropic Claude, Gemini, and OpenAI ChatGPT – so teams can create, review, and manage agreements using natural language within the tools they already use.
DOCUSIGN, INC.
•Deep integrations across business systems: Docusign integrates with core applications like Coupa, Microsoft Copilot, Salesforce, SAP, and Slack – so agreement workflows happen seamlessly across systems teams use every day, from triggering actions to surfacing completed agreements and the insights they contain.
•A connected legal AI ecosystem: Docusign is also partnering with leading legal AI platforms, including Harvey, Legora, and CoCounsel by Thomson Reuters. These integrations will bring legal research, document analysis, and contract review directly into agreement workflows across sales, procurement, HR, and finance.
Docusign IAM platform end-to-end workflows:
•IAM for HR: Employee agreements span the entire lifecycle, from hiring to role changes, but the work behind them is often fragmented and manual. IAM for HR spans the often manual HR lifecycle from hiring to role changes. Mobile I-9 verification simplifies compliance, while integrations with HCM platforms help HR teams move faster and improve the employee experience from day one onward.
•IAM for Sales: IAM for Sales brings the full agreement lifecycle directly into CRMs like HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and Salesforce. New CRM-embedded experiences for Agreement Desk, Agreement Prep, and Agreement Manager keep workflows, collaboration, and signed agreements connected in one place.
•Instant Form Creation for Customer Experience: AI-powered Web Forms transform static documents into interactive, shareable forms in seconds, so people can complete them quickly without manual re-entry.
Executive Appointment: Docusign announced Graham Sheldon as its incoming Chief Product Officer. Most recently, Sheldon served as Chief Product Officer at UiPath Inc., a leading enterprise-grade agentic automation platform. Before that, Sheldon spent more than 20 years at Microsoft Corp., including as Corporate Vice President of Product for Microsoft Teams.
